name: Nora Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We've got a hundred and fifty sows, breeding pigs, and we finish the piglets ourselves, and my husband Ivan grows barley and wheat on the other eighty hectares, most of which goes straight back into the pigs as feed. My day starts at six in the farrowing house, that's where the sows have their litters, checking for anything born overnight. Then it's feeding, cleaning out, moving pigs between sheds, and paperwork at the kitchen table after tea.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the farrowing house when it's going right, a sow lying quiet with twelve piglets lined up on her. What wears me out is the price. Pigs go up and down like a fairground ride, and when they're down you lose money on every one you sell, and the feed bill still comes in.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use much technology on the farm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The feeders in the finishing shed are automatic, Ivan put them in, and I'll admit they save my back. But I don't touch the computer side, Ivan does that. I've never used one of those AI things and I don't see what I'd ask it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the next five years, one at a time. Here's the first. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nothing much, to be honest, because it wouldn't affect me. If someone at the feed merchant's brought it up, I'd say it's fine for people in offices. I'm not one for going online and saying things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think it means nothing for us. The pig price is the thing that decides whether we have a good year, and that's set by things I can't see. Whether somebody has a clever search engine doesn't come into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. I'd keep the sows in good shape, try to keep the vet bills down, and hope the price holds up in spring. We'd keep paying the feed merchant a bit at a time, like we do, because there's not much in the bank to pay it in one go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about AI. It's the pig price that keeps me awake, same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a bad pig price year look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four years ago we lost about twenty pounds on every pig for most of a year. Ivan sold the good trailer and we didn't take a day off for eleven months. You just get your head down and wait for it to turn, because it always does, eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you pay the feed merchant a bit at a time. How does that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've had an account with Hartley's for thirty years, and old Mr Hartley's son runs it now. When things are bad he lets us run up a bill and pay it off when prices recover. That's worth more to us than any machine.

S0.say: I'd say nothing much, because it wouldn't affect me and it's fine for people in offices. I'm not one for going online and saying things.
S0.think: I really think it means nothing for us. The pig price decides our year, and a clever search engine doesn't come into it.
S0.do: Keeps the sows in good shape and tries to keep vet bills down. Keeps paying the feed merchant a bit at a time, as there isn't enough in the bank to pay it at once.
S0.feel: Calm about AI, but the pig price still keeps her awake.
S0.quote: Ivan sold the good trailer and we didn't take a day off for eleven months.
S0.fieldNote: AI barely registers for her; the pig price cycle is her whole weather system. Her safety net is a thirty-year account with the feed merchant, Hartley's. She's practical and unbothered, without strong opinions about who's to blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, there you go, it's slow, like most things. If it's taking ten years, we'll see what it's good for before we have to bother with it. I wouldn't make a fuss either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it won't reach a pig shed in my time. I'm fifty-eight, Ivan's sixty-one, and we've said we'll stop at sixty-five. The bit about fewer beginners worries me a bit, though, because nobody young wants to work with pigs already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't do anything different, I'd just carry on. Maybe if the vet started using some new system I'd go along with it, since that'd be his business. We'd start talking about what happens to the farm when we stop, which we keep putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit flat. It's not about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who helps you on the farm now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lad called Callum comes three days a week, he's twenty-four and good with pigs, which is rare. He started with us straight from school because his dad worked here before. If there are fewer beginners, the next Callum won't exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you keep putting off talking about what happens to the farm. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because neither of our girls wants it, and saying that out loud makes it real. One's a hairdresser and the other works at the bank in town. So we'd probably sell the pigs and rent the land out, and that's that.

S1.say: I'd say it's slow, like most things, and we'll see what it's good for before bothering with it. I wouldn't make a fuss either way.
S1.think: I really think it won't reach a pig shed before we stop at sixty-five. Fewer beginners worries me, since nobody young wants pig work already.
S1.do: Carries on exactly as before, going along with any new system only if the vet brings it in. Starts the long-delayed talk with Ivan about what happens to the farm when they stop.
S1.feel: Fine but a bit flat, because the picture isn't really about her.
S1.quote: If there are fewer beginners, the next Callum won't exist.
S1.fieldNote: She'd only adopt technology if someone she trusts, like the vet, made the call. Her concern is Callum, their young worker, and the lack of anyone like him in future. Succession is a sore point she's been avoiding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame for people losing jobs, and somebody should sort it out. I don't like the politicians shouting, it never helps. I'd say it at the shop counter and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm thinking of our younger girl, Katya, at the bank. Banks are all office work, and she's been worried for a while already. For the pigs, I don't see it changing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Katya to hang on to her job as long as she can, and not to go jumping around. I'd keep a bit more money back, if we could, in case she needs help with her rent. On the farm, nothing, though Ivan might get one of those assistants to do the pig movement forms, which would be fine by me if he does it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for Katya, and a bit irritated that everyone's arguing instead of fixing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said keep a bit more back. How would you manage that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd skip the holiday at Ivan's brother's, which is only a week by the coast anyway. And I'd keep the old pressure washer going another year instead of buying the new one. Little things, that's all we can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Ivan might use an assistant for the forms. Would you ever use one yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd rather sit at the table with a pen. If the form's wrong, I want to know it was me that got it wrong, not some machine I can't see.

S2.say: I'd say it's a shame for people losing jobs and somebody should sort it out. I don't like the politicians shouting, and I'd leave it at a word over the shop counter.
S2.think: I really think the pigs aren't affected, but our younger daughter Katya works at a bank. Banks are all office work, and she's already worried.
S2.do: Tells Katya to hold on to her bank job and keeps more money back in case she needs rent help. Skips the week at Ivan's brother's and runs the old pressure washer another year, leaving any AI forms to Ivan.
S2.feel: Uneasy for Katya and irritated that people argue instead of fixing things.
S2.quote: If the form's wrong, I want to know it was me that got it wrong, not some machine I can't see.
S2.fieldNote: Her centre politics come out as impatience with the arguing rather than a side. She'd let Ivan use AI but refuses it herself, wanting to own her own mistakes. Her worry is her daughter at the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a mess and they should get on and sort out a fair way of sharing it. I don't trust either side to do it well. I'd say it quietly to people I know, not in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the house prices would be the part that hits us. Both girls rent, and they'd never afford to buy. And if land prices go up, it'd make selling up worth more, but I don't want to sell to some investor who's never seen a pig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Ivan in the first few months and talk properly about what we'd sell and when, which we've been putting off. I'd help Katya if she lost her job, maybe let her stay with us. We'd carry on with the pigs, since physical work's safe in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried and a bit sad. It feels like the world's moving and we're just standing in the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want to sell to an investor. Why does that matter, if it pays more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the village is small and everyone knows the farm. If it goes to someone who puts in a manager and never shows his face, it's not a farm anymore, it's a bit of paper. I'd take a bit less to sell to someone who'd live there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said both sides can't be trusted to sort it out. What would fair look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly, I'm not clever about that. Something where people who lose their jobs get a bit of help and the rich don't get everything. That's all I'd want.

S3.say: I'd say it's a mess and they should get on and share it out fairly. I don't trust either side, and I'd say so quietly to people I know.
S3.think: I really think house prices are what would hit us, since both our daughters rent. Higher land prices would make selling pay more, but I don't want an investor who's never seen a pig.
S3.do: Sits down with Ivan within a few months to plan what they'd sell and when. Lets Katya stay if she loses her job, and keeps the pigs going since physical work is safe.
S3.feel: Worried and sad, as if the world is moving while they stand still in the yard.
S3.quote: If it goes to someone who puts in a manager and never shows his face, it's not a farm anymore, it's a bit of paper.
S3.fieldNote: She admitted she doesn't know what a fair split would look like, which felt honest. She'd take less money to sell to someone who'd live on the farm. This picture pushed her into the retirement talk she'd been avoiding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going too far, too fast, and someone ought to slow it down. I'd say I'm not having one of those in my pig sheds. I'd say it to Ivan and the vet and leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the big pig units would get robots first, and they'd produce cheaper pigs than us. We'd be pushed out on price, the way small farms always are. And Callum would be out of a job, because a robot could clean out and move pigs without needing three days a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ivan we should sell the pigs within a year rather than fight it, and rent the land out to the neighbour for the barley. I'd help Callum find work, maybe with the agricultural contractor in town. I wouldn't buy any robot, we're too close to the end and too short of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Upset, mostly for Callum. For us, it'd just bring the end forward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of your work do you think a robot would miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The listening. A poorly sow makes a different grunt, and I'll go straight to her before she gets ill. I can hear a sow going off her food from the yard. If a machine can do that, fine, but it'll have to live here first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Callum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say you're good with pigs, but you might need to be good with something else now. That'd be a hard thing to say to him, his dad worked here before him. I'd give him the best reference I've ever written.

S4.say: I'd say it's going too far, too fast, and should be slowed down. I'd tell Ivan and the vet I'm not having one in my pig sheds.
S4.think: I really think big pig units would get robots first and undercut us on price. Callum would be out of a job, since a robot could clean and move pigs.
S4.do: Tells Ivan they should sell the pigs within a year and rent the land to a neighbour for barley. Helps Callum find work with the town's agricultural contractor and buys no robot.
S4.feel: Upset, mostly for Callum, while for themselves it would just bring the end forward.
S4.quote: I can hear a sow going off her food from the yard. If a machine can do that, fine, but it'll have to live here first.
S4.fieldNote: Rather than fight, she'd quietly retire early. Her pride is in knowing her sows by sound, which she thinks no machine could learn without living there. Her grief was for Callum more than herself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, because that's the one where we'd lose the pigs early and Callum would lose his job. What would help is something for the young ones like Callum, a proper paid course in something useful. And a fair pig price, though I've been asking for that for thirty years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Hartley's, the feed merchant. If the robots come and the small farms go, Hartley's goes, and so does the account that's kept us going in the bad years. It's not just us, it's the whole chain of people who know each other.

headlineQuote: I can hear a sow going off her food from the yard. If a machine can do that, fine, but it'll have to live here first.
portrait: Nora is 58 and runs a hundred and fifty sows while her husband Ivan grows the barley and wheat that feeds them. She's never used AI, leaves the computer to Ivan and wants to own her mistakes with a pen. For most of the pictures the pig price matters more to her than AI, and her worries go to her daughters' jobs and housing and to their young worker Callum. The robot picture would make her sell the pigs early rather than fight. She'd give Callum the best reference she'd ever written.
biggestWorry: The robot picture, because they'd sell the pigs early and their young worker Callum would lose his job.
whatWouldHelp: A proper paid course for young farm workers like Callum, and a fair pig price.
